reading.title: Reading the Signs: How Trackers Find Animals
reading.purpose: Learn how trackers notice small clues and test their first guesses.
paras: A wildlife tracker can walk through a quiet forest and tell which animals passed by hours ago. This skill depends on one habit: noticing small signs that most visitors overlook. Trackers train their eyes to detect clues that sit in plain sight.

Some signs are conspicuous. A broken branch hanging at shoulder height or a flattened patch of tall grass stands out from the plants around it, so it is evident that something large passed through. Other signs are subtle, such as a few hairs caught on bark or a slightly crushed leaf.

Footprints give some of the clearest evidence, because each kind of animal leaves a distinct print. A deer leaves two split halves shaped like hearts, while a dog's print usually shows the marks of claws. A cat's print often shows no claw marks at all, because cats can pull their claws in.

Of course, not every print is easy to read. After rain, the edges blur, and an old print can become obscure, so it is hard to see or understand. Then a tracker looks for a trace, a small sign left behind, such as a nibbled nut or a feather, and tries to discern which animal made it.

Trackers also test their first guess. A rabbit track beside a fox track may suggest that the rabbit was chasing the fox, but that apparent story can be wrong. Checking the direction of the prints shows who really followed whom.
Anyone can practice. Walk slowly along a muddy path, crouch low, and look closely. The more you notice, the more the ground will tell you.

qs.q: In paragraph 4, the word "obscure" most nearly means
choices: easy to notice because it stands out strongly
left behind by a very large and heavy animal
found in the same place after every rainstorm
qs.why: The text says an old print can become obscure, "so it is hard to see or understand."

qs.q: Which sentence tells how to tell a cat's print from a dog's print?
choices: A deer leaves two split halves shaped like hearts, while a dog's print usually shows the marks of claws.
Footprints give some of the clearest evidence, because each kind of animal leaves a distinct print.
After rain, the edges blur, and an old print can become obscure, so it is hard to see or understand.
A cat's print often shows no claw marks at all, because cats can pull their claws in.
qs.why: Only this sentence tells what is different about a cat's print: it often has no claw marks.

ev.text: A cat's print often shows no claw marks at all, because cats can pull their claws in.

qs.q: Why does a tracker check the direction of the prints?
choices: To find out how heavy each animal was when it walked
To learn what time of day each of the animals passed
To make sure the first guess about the story is right
To decide which animal in the forest is the most dangerous
qs.why: The apparent story may be wrong, so the direction of the prints shows who really followed whom.

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: Only a trained expert can ever read a footprint correctly and well.
Noticing small signs helps trackers learn what animals did.
Forests are the only places where animal tracks can be found at all.
Every animal leaves the same kind of mark when it walks on mud.
qs.why: Every paragraph shows a clue or a way of checking one, and the last paragraph says the more you notice, the more you learn.

clues.text: stands out from the plants around it
a few hairs caught on bark or a slightly crushed leaf
A deer leaves two split halves shaped like hearts
